Reverse-mortgage planning: cash received, interest accumulated and home value left at sale

Track a hypothetical loan with capitalized interest, separate advances from fees, and test the home-value residual after assumed future sale costs and debt repayment.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a hypothetical loan balance with capitalized interest

Interactive planning lab

Cumulative cash advances received by the borrower$240,000
Loan balance before hypothetical repayment$583,202.27
Sale-value residual after assumed costs and loan$375,728.92

A mathematical illustration, not a reverse-mortgage quote, qualification or credit-limit calculation. Interest uses an entered effective annual rate converted to monthly compounding; it accrues before each month-end advance. Opening capitalized fees also accrue interest. There are no repayments or later fees, and all entered advances are assumed available throughout; real draw limits, rates and contract conditions can differ. Cash advances are borrowed principal, not investment income. Their subsequent spending or retention is not tracked, so this is not whole-household net worth. Sale residual is signed arithmetic before other debts, taxes, penalties or estate costs; it does not determine legal shortfall liability, contractual guarantees or an estate entitlement.

The central idea

Borrowed cash can support today’s spending while the repayment balance grows. Keep the amount received, the debt owed and the uncertain home-sale value in separate parts of the plan.

01

Put the loan proceeds and the liability in different columns

A home can be valuable while supplying little cash for monthly bills. Borrowing against it can convert some financing capacity into spendable money, but the cash arrives with a liability. A useful plan therefore tracks both the money delivered and the amount that will eventually need to be addressed.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s reverse-mortgage guide explains that interest is added to the loan and that fees may be financed or paid separately. It also describes different ways of receiving funds. Actual availability and terms depend on the agreement.

This calculator isolates those mechanics. It begins with an opening advance, adds specified fees to the loan, then assumes additional month-end advances without regular repayments. These entries are independent assumptions. The tool does not establish that a borrower qualifies or that a lender would authorize the selected cash schedule.

02

Reconcile the opening advance with financed fees

The default home value is CAD 750,000. The borrower receives CAD 150,000 at the start, while CAD 5,000 of costs are added to the opening loan. The initial liability is consequently CAD 155,000, even though the borrower receives only CAD 150,000 of cash.

Those financed fees are not an additional cash advance available for household spending. They nevertheless become part of the balance on which the hypothetical loan interest accumulates. Paying them separately would require a different opening cash plan and a smaller financed balance.

The illustration then adds CAD 500 of borrowed cash at each month-end for fifteen years. Those 180 advances total CAD 90,000. Combined with the initial cash, the borrower receives CAD 240,000 over the full period.

The amounts are nominal CAD and have not been adjusted for purchasing power. A fixed CAD 500 advance may buy less in later years. The calculator also does not assume those advances are savings: their later spending, retention or investment is outside this loan ledger.

03

Follow the compounding debt separately from cumulative cash

The selected interest assumption is a constant 7% effective annual rate. It is converted to an equivalent monthly rate using 1.07 to the power of one-twelfth, less one. Each month, interest first accrues on the opening balance; the new CAD 500 advance is then added.

After fifteen years, the modeled loan reaches approximately CAD 583,202.27. Its components are CAD 150,000 of opening cash borrowed, CAD 5,000 of financed fees, CAD 90,000 of later advances and CAD 338,202.27 of accrued interest.

The first chart compares that debt balance with cumulative cash received. The widening gap is financed fees plus interest, rather than additional spending money. A month without a regular repayment can still add to the amount owed.

The effective-rate convention is explicit so the arithmetic can be checked. A quoted product might use a different compounding convention, change rates, charge further fees or restrict advances. This model does not convert an advertisement into a contractual repayment schedule.

04

Read the future sale bridge before calling an amount equity

The independent home-value assumption is 2% growth each year. It takes CAD 750,000 to approximately CAD 1,009,401.25 after fifteen years. Hypothetical sale costs of 5% use about CAD 50,470.06, leaving CAD 958,931.19 before addressing the loan.

Subtracting the modeled CAD 583,202.27 balance leaves an arithmetic sale-value residual of approximately CAD 375,728.92. The waterfall shows the same subtraction using each component of the debt, so financed fees and later cash advances do not disappear inside a single endpoint.

This residual is not cash automatically available while the owner continues living in the home. It assumes a sale at the illustrated value and cost percentage. Other secured debts, tax, penalties, legal costs and estate obligations could require further adjustments.

Nor is it a complete household-net-worth comparison. Previously advanced money may have been spent or may still exist elsewhere. Without tracking those uses and assets, comparing only the home residual with an unborrowed home would leave out part of the household’s financial history.

05

Vary the loan rate and home-value path independently

The matrix keeps the opening home, advances, fees, horizon and sale-cost assumption fixed. Rows change annual home-value growth and columns change the effective annual loan rate. Each cell is a separate possible arithmetic path, with no probability assigned to it.

A home-value assumption does not change the loan’s compounding rate. Likewise, slower home appreciation does not automatically reduce the amount owed in the model. Keeping these assumptions independent makes the effect of each visible.

Negative residuals remain negative rather than being hidden at zero. They identify a gap between hypothetical sale proceeds and the modeled balance. They do not determine a borrower’s legal shortfall obligation or apply any contractual no-negative-equity protection. Those questions require the actual agreement and applicable rules.

Try a zero loan rate as an accounting check: the closing balance equals total cash advanced plus financed fees. That scenario isolates principal accumulation; it is not presented as an available loan offer.

06

Connect the debt projection with a dated housing and cash plan

FCAC describes repayment events including selling, moving out, the last borrower’s death and default, with timing and conditions governed by the agreement. A chosen fifteen-year chart horizon therefore cannot be treated as a guaranteed period before repayment is required.

For an actual plan, identify what could change the living arrangement, what continuing home costs remain, and how a repayment event would be funded. Confirm draw availability, interest conventions, fees and relevant conditions rather than assuming that today’s terms extend unchanged for decades.

Compare the resulting cash plan with supported alternatives, including different housing arrangements or other suitable financing. The graphs do not select an option. They make today’s borrowing and its later balance visible together, so the decision can be assessed alongside future housing needs and the resources that remain available.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original mathematical scenarios assume all entered advances remain available, a constant effective loan rate and an independently chosen home-value path. They do not assess eligibility, a lending limit, contractual guarantees or legal shortfall liability. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
